title: CMOS Logic
description: How CMOS gates are built from complementary transistors, and their noise margins, power and delay.

study.title: The CMOS inverter
study.body: A CMOS inverter is a PMOS transistor from $V_{DD}$ to the output (**pull-up**) and an NMOS transistor from the output to ground (**pull-down**), with both gates driven by the input. Input high: NMOS on, PMOS off, $V_{out} = 0$. Input low: PMOS on, NMOS off, $V_{out} = V_{DD}$. In either steady state one transistor is off, so (apart from leakage) no current flows from $V_{DD}$ to ground, and the output swings from rail to rail. The input is the insulated gate: a small capacitance, no DC current.

study.title: NAND, NOR and complex gates
study.body: NMOS transistors in the pull-down network conduct for a **1** on their gate, PMOS in the pull-up network for a **0**. The pull-up network is the **dual** of the pull-down network: series becomes parallel and vice versa, so exactly one of them conducts. NAND: NMOS in series, PMOS in parallel. NOR: NMOS in parallel, PMOS in series. An $N$-input NAND or NOR uses $2N$ transistors; series NMOS paths ANDed, parallel paths ORed, give $F = \overline{\text{pull-down function}}$.

study.title: Noise margins
study.body: The voltage transfer characteristic (VTC) gives $V_{out}$ versus $V_{in}$. A gate output guarantees at least $V_{OH}$ for a 1 and at most $V_{OL}$ for a 0; an input is safely read as 0 below $V_{IL}$ and as 1 above $V_{IH}$ (the points where the slope is −1). The **noise margins** say how much noise a signal between two gates can pick up and still be read correctly. The graph shows a simplified VTC for $V_{DD}$ = 5 V.
study.formula: \begin{array}{l} NM_L = V_{IL} - V_{OL} \\ NM_H = V_{OH} - V_{IH} \end{array}

study.title: Power dissipation
study.body: CMOS gates draw almost no **static** power (only leakage). Power is used when nodes switch: each time a load capacitance $C$ is charged to $V_{DD}$ and discharged again, an energy $CV_{DD}^2$ is taken from the supply (half is lost in the PMOS while charging, half in the NMOS while discharging). With switching frequency $f$ and activity factor $\alpha$ (fraction of nodes that switch per cycle), the **dynamic** power is below. Lowering $V_{DD}$ is the most effective way to save power. A small extra short-circuit current flows while both transistors are briefly on during an input transition.

study.title: Propagation delay and fan-out
study.body: The output needs time to charge or discharge its load through the on-resistance of a transistor. $t_{PHL}$ and $t_{PLH}$ are measured from the 50 % point of the input to the 50 % point of the output (dashed lines in the graph); $t_p \approx 0.69\,R_{on}C_L$. The load is the wiring plus the inputs of all $N$ driven gates (the **fan-out**). Because CMOS inputs draw no DC current, fan-out is limited by speed, not by current.

steps.title: Two complementary switches
steps.body: Think of the transistors as switches controlled by the gate voltage. The **NMOS** conducts when its gate is high ($V_{DD}$), the **PMOS** when its gate is low (0 V). The CMOS inverter puts a PMOS between $V_{DD}$ and the output and an NMOS between the output and ground, with one common input. For every input exactly one of them is on.

steps.prompt: The input of this CMOS inverter is high: $V_{in} = V_{DD}$. Tap the transistor that **conducts**.
steps.explanation: With $V_{GS} = V_{DD}$ the NMOS has a conducting channel and connects the output to ground, so $V_{out}$ = 0. The PMOS has its gate at the same potential as its source ($V_{SG}$ = 0), so it is off. A high input gives a low output: an inverter.

steps.prompt: The inverter input is now low ($V_{in}$ = 0 V). What happens?
steps.explanation: A low gate turns the PMOS on ($V_{SG} = V_{DD}$) and the NMOS off ($V_{GS}$ = 0). The PMOS connects the output to $V_{DD}$, so $V_{out} = V_{DD}$. Both are on only briefly while the input passes through the middle of its range.

steps.prompt: When the input of a CMOS inverter is steady (high or low), almost no current flows from the supply to ground.
steps.explanation: True. In both steady states one of the two series transistors is off, so there is no DC path from $V_{DD}$ to ground (only a tiny leakage current). That is why CMOS has very low static power: energy is used mainly when the output switches.

steps.title: The CMOS NAND gate
steps.body: A two-input NAND gate has two **NMOS in series** to ground and two **PMOS in parallel** to $V_{DD}$. The output is pulled low only if both NMOS conduct, i.e. $A = B = 1$. If either input is 0, its PMOS pulls the output high. So $F = \overline{AB}$.

steps.prompt: In this NAND gate $A$ = 1 and $B$ = 0. Tap every transistor that **conducts**.
steps.explanation: $A$ = 1 turns $N_A$ on and $P_A$ off. $B$ = 0 turns $P_B$ on and $N_B$ off. The pull-down path is broken at $N_B$ (series), while $P_B$ connects $F$ to $V_{DD}$: $F = \overline{1 \cdot 0}$ = 1.

steps.prompt: Match each network to how its transistors are connected.
steps.explanation: NAND is low only when all inputs are 1: all NMOS must conduct, so they are in series; any 0 input must pull high, so the PMOS are in parallel. NOR is low when any input is 1 (NMOS in parallel) and high only when all inputs are 0 (PMOS in series). Each pull-up network is the dual of its pull-down network.

steps.prompt: How many transistors does a static CMOS NAND gate with {{N}} inputs need?
steps.explanation: Each input drives one NMOS (in the series pull-down chain) and one PMOS (in the parallel pull-up network): $2N$ = 2 × {{N}} = **{{2*N}}** transistors.

steps.prompt: Why is the pull-up network built from PMOS and the pull-down network from NMOS transistors?
options: A PMOS turns on for a 0 and an NMOS for a 1, so for each input combination exactly one network conducts
NMOS transistors cannot be connected to the supply voltage
PMOS transistors switch faster than NMOS transistors
It halves the number of transistors
steps.explanation: The two networks must be complementary: when the pull-down conducts, the pull-up must be off and vice versa. Driving both from the same inputs works because NMOS and PMOS react oppositely to the gate voltage. (PMOS are actually **slower**, because holes are less mobile than electrons.)

steps.prompt: A CMOS output drives a load of {{C|F}} from a {{V|V}} supply. It is charged and discharged once per period of a {{f|Hz}} square wave. What is the dynamic power?
steps.explanation:
Every cycle the supply delivers $CV_{DD}^2$, so
$P = CV_{DD}^2 f$ = {{C|F}} × ({{V|V}})² × {{f|Hz}} = **{{C*V^2*f|W}}**.

steps.prompt: A processor core has a total switched capacitance of {{C|F}}, an activity factor $\alpha$ = {{a}}, $V_{DD}$ = {{V|V}} and a clock of {{f|Hz}}.

ask.prompt: What average current does it draw from the supply?
ask.explanation: $P = \alpha C V_{DD}^2 f$ = {{a*C*V^2*f|W}}, and $I = P/V_{DD} = \alpha C V_{DD} f$ = **{{a*C*V*f|A}}**.

steps.prompt: The supply voltage of a CMOS circuit is lowered from {{V1|V}} to {{V2|V}} while the clock frequency stays the same. By what percentage does the dynamic power **drop**?
steps.explanation: $P \propto V_{DD}^2$, so $P_2/P_1 = (V_2/V_1)^2$ = ({{V2}}/{{V1}})² = {{(V2/V1)^2}}. The power drops by $1 - ${{(V2/V1)^2}} = **{{100*(1-(V2/V1)^2)|%}}**. (A common mistake is to scale linearly with $V$, which gives only {{100*(1-V2/V1)|%}}.)

steps.prompt: The graph shows the (simplified) transfer characteristic of a 5 V CMOS gate.

ask.prompt: Read the levels and find the high noise margin $NM_H$.
ask.explanation: From the graph: $V_{OH}$ = {{VOH|V}} and $V_{IH}$ = {{VIH|V}}. $NM_H = V_{OH} - V_{IH}$ = **{{VOH-VIH|V}}**: a high output can drop by this much and still be read as a 1.

ask.prompt: Read the levels and find the low noise margin $NM_L$.
ask.explanation: From the graph: $V_{IL}$ = {{VIL|V}} and $V_{OL}$ = {{VOL|V}}. $NM_L = V_{IL} - V_{OL}$ = **{{VIL-VOL|V}}**: a low output can rise by this much and still be read as a 0.

steps.prompt: A ring oscillator is a loop of {{N}} inverters, each with a propagation delay of {{tp|s}}. What is its oscillation frequency?
steps.explanation: An edge must travel round the loop **twice** for one full period (once to make the output go low, once to bring it high again): $T = 2Nt_p$ = 2 × {{N}} × {{tp|s}} = {{2*N*tp|s}}, so $f = 1/T$ = **{{1/(2*N*tp)|Hz}}**. (An odd number of inverters is needed so that the loop has no stable state.)

steps.prompt: The graph shows the input and output of a CMOS inverter. The dashed lines mark 50 % of each swing and the dots where $v_{out}$ crosses it; the input edges are at $t$ = 1 ns and 6 ns. What is the average propagation delay $t_{pd}$?
steps.explanation: The falling output crosses 50 % at {{1+a}} ns: $t_{PHL}$ = {{1+a}} − 1 = {{a}} ns. The rising output crosses 50 % at {{6+b}} ns: $t_{PLH}$ = {{6+b}} − 6 = {{b}} ns. $t_{pd} = (t_{PHL} + t_{PLH})/2$ = **{{(a+b)/2}} ns**.

steps.prompt: A gate with output resistance $R_{on}$ = {{R|Ω}} drives {{N}} gate inputs of {{Cin*1e15}} fF each, plus {{Cw*1e15}} fF of wiring. Estimate its propagation delay with $t_p \approx 0.69\,R_{on}C_L$.
steps.explanation:
$C_L = C_w + N C_{in}$ = {{Cw*1e15}} fF + {{N}} × {{Cin*1e15}} fF = {{(Cw+N*Cin)*1e15}} fF.
$t_p$ = 0.69 × {{R|Ω}} × {{(Cw+N*Cin)*1e15}} fF = **{{0.69*R*(Cw+N*Cin)|s}}**. Every extra gate input on the line adds capacitance and slows the edge down.

steps.prompt: A CMOS circuit runs at a fixed clock frequency. Which graph shows how its dynamic power depends on the supply voltage $V_{DD}$?
steps.explanation: $P_{dyn} = \alpha C V_{DD}^2 f$ is proportional to $V_{DD}^2$: a parabola through the origin. Halving $V_{DD}$ quarters the power. A constant would describe static power, which in CMOS is nearly zero.

steps.prompt: When does a short-circuit current flow directly from $V_{DD}$ to ground through a CMOS inverter?
options: Briefly during an input transition, while both transistors are partly on
Only when the output is short-circuited
steps.explanation: While the input passes through the middle range ($V_{Tn} < V_{in} < V_{DD} - |V_{Tp}|$) both transistors conduct a little, and a current pulse flows straight through. Sharp input edges keep this short-circuit power small. In both steady states one transistor is off.

steps.prompt: In this NOR gate $A$ = 0 and $B$ = 1. Tap every transistor that **conducts**.
steps.explanation: $A$ = 0: $P_A$ on, $N_A$ off. $B$ = 1: $P_B$ off, $N_B$ on. The series pull-up chain is broken at $P_B$, and $N_B$ pulls the output to ground: $F = \overline{0 + 1}$ = 0.

steps.prompt: The pull-down network of a CMOS gate consists of NMOS $A$ and $B$ in **series**, and that pair in **parallel** with NMOS $C$. Which function does the gate compute?
steps.explanation: The output is pulled low when there is a conducting path to ground: through $A$ **and** $B$ (series: $AB$) **or** through $C$ (parallel: $+\,C$). A CMOS gate always inverts that condition: $F = \overline{AB + C}$, an AND-OR-INVERT gate built with only 6 transistors.

steps.prompt: What must the pull-up network of the gate $F = \overline{AB + C}$ look like?
options: PMOS $A$ and $B$ in parallel, that pair in series with PMOS $C$
PMOS $A$ and $B$ in series, that pair in parallel with PMOS $C$
steps.explanation: The pull-up network is the dual of the pull-down network: swap series and parallel. Check: the output must be high when $\overline{AB + C} = (\overline{A} + \overline{B})\,\overline{C}$ = 1, i.e. ($A$ = 0 **or** $B$ = 0) **and** $C$ = 0: $P_A \parallel P_B$, in series with $P_C$.

steps.prompt: In static CMOS an AND gate is built as a NAND gate followed by an inverter. How many transistors does a {{N}}-input AND gate need?
steps.explanation: The {{N}}-input NAND needs $2N$ = {{2*N}} transistors and the inverter 2 more: **{{2*N+2}}**. CMOS logic is naturally inverting, which is why NAND/NOR are the basic gates and AND/OR cost extra.

steps.require: min(floor((tmax/(0.69*R) - Cw)/Cin) - 0.5, min((tmax/(0.69*R) - Cw)/Cin - floor((tmax/(0.69*R) - Cw)/Cin) - 0.1, 0.9 - ((tmax/(0.69*R) - Cw)/Cin - floor((tmax/(0.69*R) - Cw)/Cin))))
steps.prompt: A gate with $R_{on}$ = {{R|Ω}} drives a line with {{Cw*1e15}} fF of wiring capacitance. Each gate input on the line adds {{Cin*1e15}} fF. With $t_p \approx 0.69\,R_{on}C_L$, what is the largest fan-out $N$ for which $t_p \le$ {{tmax|s}}?
steps.explanation: The allowed load is $C_{L,max} = t_{max}/(0.69R_{on})$ = {{tmax|s}}/(0.69 × {{R|Ω}}) = {{tmax/(0.69*R)*1e15||4}} fF. Subtract the wiring: {{(tmax/(0.69*R)-Cw)*1e15||4}} fF is left for inputs, i.e. {{(tmax/(0.69*R)-Cw)/Cin||4}} inputs. Round **down**: $N$ = **{{floor((tmax/(0.69*R)-Cw)/Cin)}}**.

steps.prompt: To save battery, a phone processor switches from {{V1|V}} at full clock speed to a mode with $V_{DD}$ = {{V2|V}} and the clock divided by {{k}}. What is the new dynamic power, as a percentage of the original?
steps.explanation: $P \propto V_{DD}^2 f$: $P_2/P_1 = (V_2/V_1)^2 \cdot (f_2/f_1)$ = ({{V2}}/{{V1}})² × 1/{{k}} = **{{100*(V2/V1)^2/k|%}}**. Reducing $f$ alone saves a factor {{k}}; lowering the voltage (possible because the slower clock tolerates longer delays) saves another factor {{(V1/V2)^2}}.

steps.prompt: For the same number of inputs, a CMOS NAND gate is usually faster than a NOR gate.
steps.explanation: True. A NOR gate has its **PMOS** in series, and PMOS transistors are slower (hole mobility is roughly 2–3 times lower than electron mobility). A NAND puts the faster NMOS in series and the PMOS in parallel. That is why NAND-based logic is preferred.

steps.prompt: A CMOS output with load capacitance {{C|F}} is charged from 0 to $V_{DD}$ = {{V|V}} and then discharged to 0 again.

ask.prompt: How much energy does the supply deliver during this full cycle?
ask.explanation: While charging, a charge $Q = CV_{DD}$ flows from the supply at voltage $V_{DD}$: $E = QV_{DD} = CV_{DD}^2$ = {{C|F}} × ({{V|V}})² = **{{C*V^2|J}}**. During discharge the supply delivers nothing.

ask.prompt: How much energy is dissipated in the PMOS transistor while the load charges?
ask.explanation: The supply delivers $CV_{DD}^2$ while charging, but only $\frac{1}{2}CV_{DD}^2$ ends up stored in the capacitor. The other half, **{{C*V^2/2|J}}**, is lost in the PMOS on-resistance (whatever its value). The stored half is later dissipated in the NMOS during discharge.
